title: How Do Habits Form?
paragraphs: A large part of what we do each day is not the result of careful decisions but of habits. We make coffee, check our messages or take the same way to work almost automatically, which saves the brain a lot of effort.

Psychologists often describe a habit as a loop with three parts: a cue, a routine and a reward. The cue is a signal, such as a time, a place or a feeling. The routine is the behaviour itself, and the reward is the pleasant result that follows.

Each time the loop is repeated, the link between the cue and the routine becomes stronger. Eventually, the cue alone is enough to start the behaviour, even when we do not really want the reward any more. This is why bad habits can be so hard to stop.

Building a good habit takes patience. In a well-known study from University College London, it took participants 66 days on average for a new daily behaviour to become automatic, although the time varied a lot from person to person. Starting small and linking the new habit to an existing cue can help.
